This is filmslop: a terrible movie masked by good production and the illusion of progressivism. Like One Battle After Another (OBAA), this movie takes a very surface-level approach to addressing progressive issues. It uses imagery inspired by the events that took place in District Six, when 60,000 Black South Africans were forcibly removed from their homes and relocated by the Apartheid Government. Furthermore, this movie depicts police brutality, medical torture, xenophobia, segregation, corporate abuse, war profiteering, and more. However, like OBAA, its purpose is to create surface-level sympathy for the aliens and obstacles for our MC, instead of interrogating these issues, their effects, and using them to reflect the ills of our society. This film tries to pull a white-saviour story on us, but utterly fails because of how EVIL our MC is. MC is a horrible person from the get-go; he's a depraved, power-hungry psychopath who only sides with the aliens because he needs to, not because he wants to. He never grows in this story, staying the same miserable human he always was. As for the aliens, how we're meant to see them and how they're depicted are very different. On one hand, they display humanity, with relationships, worries, and feelings, but on the other hand, you can't help but understand the actions of our villains, as the aliens are only depicted as crazed maniacs, and any facts given to us only reinforce these views, instead of debunking them. Its depictions of Nigerians are very racist. This film plays into racist caricatures of Nigerians, viewing them as violent scammers who believe in nonsensical rituals, when this is clearly not the case. The tone is all over the place. I have no idea what I'm supposed to feel in any given moment, and I don't think this movie does either. For example, at the start, it tries to balance its very dark depictions of the beginnings of forced resettlement with humour, but fails miserably as it doesn't know when to stop being comedic or dark. There are also many plot holes apparent in this film, relating to the aliens, the authoritarian company that manages District 9 and more. This adds more layers of confusion to an already confusing mess of a film. In conclusion, this film is SO BAD.

I distinctly remember seeing District 9 in theaters in 2009 and disliking it. Given the overwhelming praise it received, I always wondered whether I had missed something? After finally revisiting it all these years later, I’m convinced that my initial reaction was correct: District 9 isn’t good. The film fails for me in two main areas: story and style. Narratively, it presents itself as an intelligent, original piece of high-concept science fiction, but it’s really anything but. The apartheid allegory is immediately obvious and handled with very little subtlety. Beyond that, the plot becomes repetitive and never develops into anything especially compelling. Wikus is also a weak and passive protagonist, which makes it difficult to invest in his transformation or care about what happens to him. Stylistically, the film combines documentary and found-footage techniques, but neither approach is convincing. The multiple camera angles, conspicuously scripted interviews, and constant shifts in perspective prevent it from ever feeling like an authentic documentary. It also repeatedly uses the “blood on the lens technique” every time someone gets shot, which gets old incredibly quickly. With an unsubtle and unengaging narrative, ugly visuals, unconvincing presentation, and a protagonist I couldn’t root for, I’m left wondering what the film is actually offering? Ultimately, not much.

There are things about the first half of District 9 that I found interesting. The mockumentary format works well, and the film’s depiction of bureaucracy, forced relocation, and casual dehumanization gives it a more interesting foundation than where the movie ultimately finishes. I really struggled with the apartheid allegory at the center of it. I understand the commentary the film is attempting to make, but drawing such an explicit parallel between the victims of South African apartheid and a population of literal aliens feels like a strange and uncomfortable comparison. I understand what the film is reaching for, but I could not get past the feeling that framing such a horrific and very real history through this particular comparison risks delegitimizing some of its horrors rather than meaningfully illuminating them. I also found Wikus difficult to invest in for much of the movie. His eventual empathy feels less like a genuine reckoning with the cruelty he has participated in and more like something forced upon him once he begins experiencing that cruelty himself. There are interesting ideas here, and I understand why the film has endured, but I was much more interested in the movie District 9 seemed to be during its first act. By the time it turns into a fairly conventional action sci-fi movie, a lot of what initially made it interesting gets lost. I kept wishing it would return to the questions it had raised instead of shooting its way through them.

It's insane to me that the humans in this movie apparantly never asked the aliens whether they knew how to get their spaceship working again...!? I suppose they were just that racist. How hard is it to understand that a species capable of building intergalactic vessels is incredibly intelligent? In that sense, I don't quite buy the desolate state of human-alien relations here, seeing as they were seemingly able to understand eachother. Or wait, did Wikus only become able to speak with them after his contamination? I'm not sure, but that'd make more sense. I gotta give it to them, it was inspired to make a movie where the aliens don't invade earth but are at the mercy of humans. The initial mockumentary format was neat, and I lost interest in the movie more as it shifted from social commentary to CGI-splatter action. The film ought to have focused on its unique themes and core idea, not to compete with other sci-fi movies by going all in on the action. The explody fighting was one thing that made me consider the film a bit crass. The aliens themselves were a little silly looking but largely inoffensive graphics-wise. I got used to them. Over-eager and simple Wikus was also a kind of funny but fairly unlikeable lead. It's also a pretty funny name to me. Wikus. Wikus. Makes me laugh tbh, sorry Wikuses! xD The movie basically explores what it'd take for Adolf Eichmann to put himself in the shoes of the people he rules over and have some empathy. The picture proposes that what it takes is getting put in the same boat with them, becoming one of them, as it were. Maybe one should go and live among th e marginalized community before passing judgement on them. Still, the film reveals a lack of vision by having the solution seemingly be to just send the asylum seekers back. Futhermore, it feels as though Wikus ultimately does the right thing only begrudgingly when his conscience can no longer be ignored. He helps the one alien he personally knows and is friends with, because it's become undeniable he has an obligation to. That's how it goes, but Wikus also only makes this choice when he's in his super mech -- protected and empowered to blast enemies to shreds -- when it's additionally quite clear he can't get what he wants anyway. This makes his redemption a little weak. The banality of evil becomes the banality of good. A lack of nuanced characters hampers the movie's ability to speak on issues around immigration and tolerance. With the terrible anti-immigrant riots taking place in South Africa as one example, I would have wished the movie to pack a little more punch. The immigrant stand-in aliens don't have much agency at all, getting shafted as characters for Wikus to have his white saviour moment, while the antagonists are so over-the-top evil that they won't make anybody reflect on themselves. As the villains we've got soldiers so unapologetically hyped about killing aliens that anybody could tell they were fascists, and cannibalistic Nigerian gangsters so offensive the movie was banned in Nigeria. Usar la metamorfosis para mostrar cómo el gobierno experimenta con él para sacar provecho armamentístico es más interesante. As much as this movie is celebrated as one of the most innovative science fiction films of the 2000s, it’s a movie I really didn’t like when it came out and have never warmed to since. Part of is the premise—aliens arrive on Earth and the first act of the government is to quarantine them—which is both an embarrassingly obvious apartheid parallel and an unenjoyably cynical interpretation of first contact. No one in the film is particularly likable, with protagonist Sharlto Copley a hapless middle manager rarely in control of events and all the non-alien characters being cartoonishly evil. It’s also an ugly movie to watch, between the mock documentary setup and the washed-out industrial desert palate, visuals and camerawork that gives me a headache the longer it goes on. I’ll award it some points for  character and technology design, particularly in the final mech fight where you get some cathartic vengeance against the soldiers. It’s possible I just don’t vibe with Neil Blomkamp’s vision, having similarly bumped up against Elysium and Chappie for the same reasons of finding them too dark and unsubtle, but I truly don’t get the place that this occupies in the sci-fi hierarchy.

It wants to be a political movie about apartheid, so it's set in South Africa. But it doesn't have anything to say about actual, real life South African apartheid and it's legacy, so the profoundly poignant history of the setting is ignored, and South Africa just becomes a vaguely impoverished, multiracial backdrop. There are implied economic differences between the Black and white South Africans, but nothing political. The story is about an entirely fictional apartheid, with no care for how the situation would intersect with the actual history of a recently overthrown apartheid regime, and so what should have been an evocative setting winds up coming across as rather tone deff, in a way that it wouldn't have if the movie were just set in Europe. The movie is set in 2008, which means that the mothership would have landed in 1988 . . . six years before South African apartheid fucking ended. And I want it said that I like this movie! It's an interesting and entertaining work of science fiction, that inverts a lot of alien invasion tropes in a way that I find compelling. I just can't get over the superficially woke ignorance of its political framing. As much as I enjoy forwardly political movies, I feel like District 9 is at its best when it's not trying to make obviouse real-world comparisons—the premise is political enough, we don't need to see the Black South African masses marching through the streets calling for apartheid!

There’s something fascinating about the movie’s strange sense of realism. Of course, the story itself is completely unrealistic, but the movie is remarkably meticulous in its pursuit of realism. The documentary-style direction is part of it, but so are all the carefully prepared details: the derogatory terms used for the aliens, the justifications put forward by the corporations, the human-rights organizations, and so on. All of these little touches make the world feel much more real. The visual quality is excellent, too. Whether it’s the sight of a gigantic UFO hovering over the city or the scenes inside the alien settlement, everything feels surprisingly natural and never out of place. That’s actually quite an achievement. And although it’s a little grotesque, I also liked the technique of having bits of flesh occasionally splatter against the camera lens. It’s a simple but very effective touch.

Sci-fi action movie filmed primarily in a mockumentary/found footage style, but it intermittently breaks from that to a traditional 3rd person narrative and even uses news broadcast blurbs at times. The format switches work very well. The unknown cast adds realism to the mockumentary style. It’s a good story, a fresh take on first contact and a brutally honest portrayal of how humanity would probably react. Heavily themed on Apartheid and racial injustice, while also taking aim at corporate greed and the global military industrial complex. A subplot has a ruthless corporate executive openly plotting against his own son in law. The irony of the main character having to lose his humanity to become humane parallels the viewer’s transformation to rooting for the aliens by the third act. Excellent cgi effects for the aliens and alien technology, and practical body horror. While the sci-fi elements and themes are prevalent, this is first and foremost an action movie. Hardly a dull moment.

It’s an action alien movie with crazy weapons and a fair amount of gore, but it’s not your stereotypical action alien movie with crazy weapons and a fair amount of gore. I simultaneously love the story and am pretty pissed off by the story (complimentary). Like I’ve questioned before with movies, including my beloved Arrival , why is mankind so quick to assume the worst intent from those not like us? Why must we always seek self-gain at the expense of others? My main critique is the way in which our main character develops; it’s a fairly common trope that I saw coming from a mile away and didn’t add much substance for me. I have ideas on how I would’ve liked to have seen District 9 end, but we deal with what we’re dealt. Other than that, I love the action, I love the effects, I love the themes and social commentary, and I wish I hadn’t waited years to watch.

Still a very good film after a long time since the first watch. District 9 really performs well by being so different from most Sci-Fi films. It dives much deeper into it's themes and messaging, (Which are all the more relevant today as they were in 2009), Which makes this film come off powerful. Which I can't really say I've felt before with a Sci-Fi film. Blomkamp has very interesting ideas, Which I love! The more originality the better! And while I've heard Elysium was a good step down, And I personally remember not being the biggest fan of Chappie, At least I can appreciate that they feel like passion projects for Blomkamp. District 9 is no different. You can tell he really cared about this film, And just makes the film feel so well directed. Also I gotta mention one of my all time favorite actors Sharlto Copley! Who fuckin aces this film! He is so fuckin good! Also gotta mention the special effects which still for the most part hold up super well, And it's just so mind boggling it was filmed with such a lower budget! Overall, District 9 is a powerful and really well crafted Sci-Fi. Definitely worth a watch if you haven't seen it yet! ................................................................
